title: Build a biosand filter
summary: A tall container of sieved, washed sand over gravel, kept under a 5 cm layer of standing water, grows a living layer that takes out most germs and cloudiness with no power and nothing to replace. It needs up to a month to ripen and daily use, freezing cuts its germ removal and drying out harms the living layer, and the water still needs disinfecting after it.

materials.item: Watertight, rust-proof, non-toxic container about 90 cm (3 ft) tall: a new or food-grade plastic drum, for example, never one that held chemicals
Filtration sand that passes a 0.7 mm sieve, crushed rock best
materials.qty: about 30 L for a CAWST-size filter, more for a wider drum

materials.item: Plastic outlet tube, 6 mm (1/4 in) bore, 9 mm (3/8 in) outside
materials.qty: about 1 m (CAWST cuts about 105 cm for its own filter; measure yours)

materials.item: Diffuser: plastic or galvanised sheet drilled with 3 mm holes on a 2.5 cm grid
Sieves of 12 mm, 6 mm, 1 mm and 0.7 mm mesh: metal wire screen on a wood frame (0.7 mm is #24 mesh); nylon and fibreglass tear
Clean water for washing the media and flushing the filter
materials.qty: plenty for washing, plus 40–80 L to flush the filter

materials.item: Covered storage container with a tap, for the filtered water
Plain unscented bleach, for disinfecting the filtered water and the outlet
Dust mask for sieving dry crushed rock

steps.text: Pick its spot first: inside the heated part of the house, level, out of reach of frost, where you'll use it every day. Move the empty container there before it's filled (CAWST manual).
steps.warn: A filled filter is far too heavy to move: CAWST's concrete one weighs 95 kg plus 45 kg of sand (CAWST manual). A 57 cm drum of sand 54 cm deep holds about 200 kg of sand (estimate from CAWST's 45 kg per 30 L): use a solid floor.

steps.text: Sieve the sand through 12, 6, 1 and 0.7 mm screens in that order. Keep 6–12 mm for drainage gravel, 1–6 mm for separating gravel, and everything finer than 0.7 mm as filtration sand (CAWST manual).
steps.warn: Wear an N95 or better mask, outdoors if you can: dry rock dust can hold silica ([silica card](#browse/hazards/silica)). CAWST says damp sand plugs the screens and wet-sieves with clean water only when sand can't be dried (CAWST manual).

steps.text: Wash the gravel a little at a time until the water runs clear. Wash the sand by swirling it with twice its volume of water and pouring off the dirty water, but stop while the water is still a bit cloudy (CAWST manual).

Jar-test the sand: put some sand and an equal amount of clear water in a jar with a lid and swirl it; 3–4 seconds after you stop, you should just see the sand surface (CAWST manual). Count your washes so you can repeat them.

Fit the outlet tube from the bottom centre of the container, up the side and out. Set the end of the outlet so it sits 5 cm above where the top of the sand will be: the standing water settles at the height of the outlet's end (CAWST manual).
steps.warn: Never fit a hose or tap to the outlet or plug it. A hose can siphon the filter dry, and a plug drowns the living layer (CAWST manual).

steps.text: Half fill the container with water, then add 5 cm (2 in) of drainage gravel over the outlet, level it, and add 5 cm of separating gravel on top (CAWST manual).
Pour in the washed sand quickly, keeping water above it the whole time, so no air pockets form and the grain sizes stay mixed (CAWST manual).

Fill with water, let it run until it stops, and measure the water over the sand. Add or take out sand until it is 5 cm (2 in) deep; 4–6 cm is acceptable (CAWST manual). Swirl the top of the sand, scoop off the muddy water and level the surface.
Make the diffuser: 3 mm holes on a 2.5 cm grid, fitting tight to the walls with no gap, and sitting above the standing water, not in it (CAWST manual).

With the diffuser in place, flush with the cleanest water you have (under 50 NTU) until it comes out clear, usually 40–80 L. If it still isn't clear after 100 L the gravel was too dirty: take it out, wash it and start again (CAWST manual).

Time the flow with the reservoir full. CAWST's filter should give no more than 0.4 L a minute (CAWST manual). CAWST says a plastic filter may have different numbers (CAWST fact sheet), so for a drum 400 L an hour per square metre of sand surface, the rate of CAWST's concrete filter, is only a rough estimate. Faster than that, the sand was washed too much and the filter may not clean well: replace the sand and wash it less (CAWST manual).

Use it at least once a day, with the same source each time. Strain or settle water before it goes in if it is cloudier than 50 NTU (CAWST manual, CAWST fact sheet). Always pour through the diffuser, never straight onto the sand.
Wait at least 1 hour after the water stops flowing before the next batch, and never more than 48 hours; 6–12 hours is best (CAWST fact sheet).
Disinfect everything it makes, by boiling or chlorine in the storage container, and especially in the first month and after each cleaning (CAWST manual).
steps.warn: Never pour chlorine into the filter itself: it kills the living layer (CAWST manual, WHO chlorine test). Chlorine is weak against Cryptosporidium, so boil instead if it may be in the source (WHO chlorine test).

steps.text: When the flow becomes too slow for you, CAWST's sign for its own filter being under 0.1 L a minute, do a swirl and dump: take out the diffuser, swirl only the very top of the sand by hand, scoop the dirty water out and dump it outside the house in a soak pit or garden, level the sand, refit the diffuser and refill (CAWST manual). Wash your hands after.

notes:
## How it works
A biosand filter is a household version of the slow sand filters towns have used for a long time, built to be filled in batches rather than run all the time (CAWST manual). Germs and dirt are caught between sand grains, stick to them, are eaten by other microbes, or die off. The work is done mostly by a living layer, the biolayer or schmutzdecke, in the top 1–2 cm of the sand, which needs oxygen: it gets it from the water you pour in, and between batches from the air through the standing water (CAWST manual, CAWST fact sheet). Lower down there's so little food and oxygen that virtually nothing lives (CAWST manual).

The 5 cm of standing water is the key number. Deeper water lets less oxygen through and thins the biolayer; shallower water can dry it out (CAWST manual).

## What it removes
| | Lab | Field | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bacteria | up to 96.5 % | 87.9–98.5 % | CAWST manual |
| Viruses | 70 to over 99 % | no figure | CAWST manual |
| Protozoa | over 99.9 % | no figure | CAWST manual |
| Cloudiness | 95 %, under 1 NTU | 85 % | CAWST manual |
| Dissolved chemicals | not effective | | CAWST fact sheet |

Without a mature biolayer it removes only about 30–70 % of germs; with one, up to 99 % (CAWST manual). That's a big help, not a guarantee, so **disinfect the output every time** (CAWST manual): boil, or chlorinate it in the storage container. Chlorine is ineffective against Cryptosporidium (WHO chlorine test), so boil instead if it may be in the source water. The filter makes chlorine work better, because it clears the cloudiness germs hide behind (CAWST manual). Use plain unscented bleach only, never mixed with ammonia, vinegar or other acids, or toilet cleaners (see [Chemicals](#guides/reference_chemicals)). For bleach doses see [Two-bucket gravity filter](#guides/build_gravity_water_filter); for what other filters do, [Water filters](#guides/reference_water_filters). WHO's advice is the same from the other side: chlorine goes in after a slow sand or other biological stage, never before it (WHO chlorine test).

## CAWST's numbers (Version 10 concrete filter)
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Height | 940 mm |
| Filtration sand | under 0.7 mm, 543 mm deep |
| Separating gravel | 1–6 mm, 50 mm deep |
| Drainage gravel | 6–12 mm, 50 mm deep |
| Standing water over the sand | 5 cm (4–6 cm) |
| Reservoir | 12 L, the same as the water held in the sand's pores |
| Flow with the reservoir full | no more than 0.4 L/min |
| Loading rate | no more than 400 L per hour per m² of sand |
| Pause between batches | 1–48 hours |
| Batch | 12–18 L; 24–72 L a day at 4 batches |

Sources: CAWST manual; batch sizes and the 6–12 hour best pause from the CAWST fact sheet. CAWST's fact sheet says not more than 600 L/h/m², while its manual says 400 for this Version 10 design and lists 0.6 L a minute for the older Versions 8 and 9 (CAWST manual, CAWST fact sheet). Use the lower one.

## Other containers
CAWST says the body can be concrete, plastic or any other watertight, rust-proof, non-toxic material, and notes that a plastic filter may have different operating numbers from the concrete one (CAWST fact sheet). CDC advises food-grade containers and none that ever held toxic chemicals (CDC water storage). CAWST's fact sheet says a plastic filter's outlet pipe is external, can be damaged or leak, and is hard to repair once broken (CAWST fact sheet). CAWST details only its concrete filter, so the drum layout in the steps and what follows are rough estimates, not CAWST's figures. Keeping CAWST's depths and grain sizes and borrowing its 400 L/h/m² rate, a drum 57 cm across inside has about 0.26 m² of sand surface and would allow about 100 L an hour, roughly 1.7 L a minute with the reservoir full. It would also hold about 140 L of sand, roughly 200 kg by CAWST's ratio of 45 kg to 30 L, and can't be moved once filled.

CAWST ranks sand sources: crushed rock first; then sand from high on a riverbank; then riverbed sand; beach sand last. River sand carries germs and leaves, which can make the water worse than it went in, and beach sand carries salt (CAWST manual).

## Ripening and daily use
- **First month:** the biolayer takes up to 30 days to form. The water can be used meanwhile, but disinfect it (CAWST manual).
- **Every day:** use it at least once a day, ideally 2–4 times, from the same source; a new source takes the biolayer several days to adjust to (CAWST manual).
- **Lid on, diffuser in, outlet free:** never pour onto bare sand, never store food on the diffuser, and never plug the outlet or fit a hose to it (CAWST manual).
- **Storage:** catch the water in a clean covered container with a tap, and clean the outlet with soap or chlorine solution now and then (CAWST manual).
- **Slower isn't worse:** a slow filter is still cleaning well; the swirl and dump is for convenience, and the biolayer needs time to recover after it, so disinfect the output meanwhile (CAWST manual).

## Winter
A biosand filter is alive, and cold is its enemy. In a Michigan Tech study, filters in colder rooms first removed fewer coliforms and E. coli, then caught up as they adapted; filters that were frozen and thawed all lost a significant share of their germ removal, the hardest-frozen most (Arnold cold BSF). So:
- keep it inside the home (CAWST manual), in a room that stays above freezing;
- if it freezes or dries out, play safe and treat it as a new filter: flush it and disinfect everything it makes for up to 30 days, the time CAWST gives for a living layer to form (CAWST manual). You can't check the biolayer by looking: it isn't visible (CAWST manual).

Disinfect the output however cold it is, and remember chlorine works more slowly in cold water: at 18 °C and above give it at least 30 minutes, and longer when colder (WHO chlorine test).
